newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: JOBS - Multinationals, tax ease Irish black spot.
newsitem.headline: JOBS - Multinationals, tax ease Irish black spot.

text.p: DUBLIN, March 5, Reuter - "We fully recognise the unprecedented growth in job creation in Ireland in recent years."
These are not the words of a political party on the vote trail, a business think-tank or European Union study into the Irish economy.
They are an unbegrudging salute from the Irish National Organisation for the Unemployed, a pressure group built on the foundations of a country once mired in unemployment.

It still campaigns for special help for the long-term unemployed, people who have been out of work for three or more years, but it readily acknowledges that the national dole queue is getting steadily shorter. Unemployment was the Irish black spot. Ten years ago the Irish were leaving their homeland in record numbers to seek work in foreign countries.

Today net migration is almost nil. Unemployment has dipped from 17 percent to just under 12 and is still falling, while economic giants like Germany grapple with the problem for the first time in decades.
Ten years ago the only chips people talked about in Ireland were the ones they cut from potatoes, deep fried and served with sausages or battered fish.

Today there is hardly a multinational computer company that has not set up in Ireland. If the government had its way, Intel Corp's "Intel inside" logo would also say, "Made In Ireland." Record growth, tax breaks for multinationals and a crackdown on dole fraud have combined to lift the stain of unemployment from Ireland's curriculum vitae.

The arrival of a new multinational or creation of a handful of jobs used to be a top news item. "These days it's an everyday occurrence," said a spokesman for IDA Ireland, the government's investment agency.
IRISH GROWTH BUCKS EUROPEAN TREND
While other European Union economies went into recessionary reverse in the 1990s, Ireland's shifted into overdrive reaching growth rates of 10 per cent.
"This exceptionally strong economic performance has resulted in phenomenal employment growth," said Ireland's Economic and Social Research Institute.
"Total employment increased by an average of over 45,000 per year between 1993 and 1996 while unemployment declined from almost 17 percent in 1993 to just under 13 percent in 1996," it said.

Prime Minister John Bruton had only to drive 100 miles (160 km) to be in part of Britain - Northern Ireland - and use the occasion on Friday to vaunt the comparative track records of the two countries.
"The real growth in the (Irish) Republic's economy in 1995 was five times and last year was four times that of the United Kingdom" he said in a speech.
"The annual percentage increase in employment has also been significantly faster than that of the UK, six times in 1996 and eight times faster last year."
Bruton and most analysts trace Ireland's transformation from a marginal, largely agricultural backwater to economic success story to the rapid growth of education in the 1960s.
This produced an English-speaking workforce ready to slot into jobs the government canvassed in the multinational electronics and pharmaceutical sectors.
"There was a close synchronisation between the industries attracted from overseas and the investments we were making in education," Bruton said.

European Union membership in 1973 opened up markets and an aid tap that is still open, subsidising every Irish family to the tune of 2,000 Irish pounds ($3,150) a year, according to unofficial estimates.
Under EU rules, Ireland qualifies for grants and aid to help its economy catch up with the strongest in the EU and this has also permitted it to offer special tax incentives to overseas investors.
The IDA offers a 10 per cent corporation tax under a dispensation that is scheduled to expire in 2010 but which has managed to attract a Whos' Who of the world's leading electronics companies.

"With three very strong years behind us, Ireland has become for the first time the market leader of US companies undertaking greenfield investment into Europe," IDA Chief Executive Kieran McGowan said.
IRELAND VIEWED AS GATEWAY TO EUROPE
Intel, Seagate Technology, Hewlett-Packard, Gateway 2000 and IBM were among dozens of overseas investors seizing Ireland as a venue for production and gateway to Europe.
Trade Unions too have been brought into the business of shaping the economy through a series of national pay agreements which have slashed the number of days lost each year through work stoppages.

Bruton's government has also seized the opportunity to launch an unprecedented crackdown on social security fraud to catch people claiming unemployment benefit who are actually at work in the black economy.
The net result on the jobless tally has still be to computed but analysts believe it is a contributory factor to the monthly improvements in the number of people claiming benefit.

"I won't be able to come in to work on Thursday afternoon because I have to go and get my dole money," is a phrase the Department of Social Welfare hopes will pass into folklore. ($ = 0.633 Irish Pounds)
